title: Bureau 1440
text:
### Rassvet-1

Three Rassvet-1 spacecraft were launched into an orbit at an altitude of 588.4 km and an inclination of 98° on a Soyuz-2.1b launch vehicle from the Vostochny Cosmodrome on June 27, 2023. The spacecraft separated from the upper stage as scheduled, completed their flight sequence, and came under the control of Bureau 1440 Mission Control Center (its own ground segment, during the experimental launches, included five tracking stations distributed across Russia).[1,2] The mission was designed to experimentally test key satellite technologies and components in various scenarios.[3,4] The Rassvet-1 spacecraft were developed in just three years. Their mass was virtually identical to that of PS-1—about 80 kg.[5]

Over the course of several months, Bureau 1440 experimentally tested communications between ground subscribers (data download speed from the satellite was 48 Mbit/s with a latency of 38 ms, and transmission speed was 12 Mbit/s with a latency of 42 ms),[6,7] the operation of propulsion systems, and other methods of adjusting satellite orbits.[8] In August 2023, during a demonstration of satellite communications technology, Russian Deputy Prime Minister Dmitry Chernyshenko held a video call from the Mission Control Center in Moscow with the Minister of Digital Development of Adygea, Zaurbek Shu, who was located on Mount Fisht, outside the coverage area of mobile networks.[9]

### Rassvet-2

Three Rassvet-2 satellites were launched on the night of May 16–17, 2024, from the Plesetsk Cosmodrome. With an updated payload and new instruments, the satellites were twice the size of the first mission's satellites. They were equipped with laser communication terminals and satellite communications equipment developed by Bureau 1440 using the 5G NTN protocol standard.[10,11]

During the Bureau 1440 mission, 5G communications technology was tested (the company claimed to have overcome the Doppler effect and delays in the communication channel between the subscriber terminal and the satellite, which was moving at a speed of 27,000 km/h at an altitude of 800 km). During the inter-satellite laser communications tests, 14 tests were conducted at distances of 30–220 km, with a total of 1.5 terabytes of data transmitted (the maximum volume in a single session was 450 GB without damaged packets).[12,13,14]

### Rassvet-3

Rassvet-3 is intended to provide a commercial system, the Rassvet broadband network. Rassvet-3 satellites have a mass of about 370 kilogram operating in a near-polar orbit at inclination 82.3 degrees, intended to provide a near-global service including in the arctic. They have krypton propellant electric thrusters and laser inter-satellite links.[15,16] The satellites are in low Earth orbit at an altitude of about 800 km. The Rassvet website states that user terminals use an active phased array antenna and have "data rates up to 1 Gbps and latency under 70 ms."[17,18]

The first launch of Rassvet-3 satellites took place on 23 March 2026 aboard a Soyuz 2.1b / Fregat-M launch vehicle from Plesetsk Cosmodrome.[19,20,21,22]

In July, Russian sources reported that the altitude of the constellation had been revised to an altitude of approximately 500 km.[23] Additionally, the satellite Rassvet-3 10, which was initially expected to decay, began climbing again to reach the constellation.[24] On 19 July 2026, a second batch of 16 satellites were launched aboard a Soyuz 2.1b launch vehicle from Plesetsk Cosmodrome.[24]

In late August 2026, the Institute for the Study of War expressed doubts about the viability program, stating that only 37.5 percent of satellites had reached "sustainable operational altitudes", referring to the originally declared altitude of 800 km.[25,26] However, an article in Ars Technica stated that it was too early to definitively come to this conclusion.[27]

As of 7 October 2026, it was reported that, of the batch of 32 Rassvet-3 satellites, 17 satellites had reached a holding altitude of 510 km, with nine more at altitudes between 446 and 498 km.[28] A further five occupied altitudes between 253 - 375 km. One satellite (Rassvet-3 4) had been lost as a result of orbital decay in June 2026.

Partial service is expected to start in 2027, a Russia-wide service by 2030, and be extended to full coverage by 2035.[16,18] In July 2026, the Rassvet website stated that 156 satellites are planned to be in orbit by the end of 2026, 292 by 2027, 610 by 2028, growing to 900 by 2035.[29] It is believed satellite to user terminal communication will use 5G NTN technology.[30]
